items.title: Pharmeasy’s owner, API Holdings, has sold nearly 20% of Thyrocare over the past year to repay debt, while still retaining control of the diagnostics ...
items.description_html:
Pharmeasy’s owner, API Holdings, has sold nearly 20% of Thyrocare over the past year to repay debt, while still retaining control of the diagnostics company.

Pharmeasy bought Thyrocare in 2021, eventually owning about 71%.

It sold about 10% in October 2025 and another 10% last week, raising Rs 1,654 crore across the two sales. Its stake in Thyrocare is now down to 51%.

The money from the latest stake sale has been used by API Holdings to repay Rs 1,050 crore debt held through NCDs.

With this, privately held API Holdings says it has become debt-free.

Over the last 4-5 years, API had to go through a massive down round at a 90% valuation cut, from $5.6 billion to less than $500 million, in order to repay debt. It had also earlier sold its stake in software firm Marg ERP.

RT Pratik Bhakta
The RBI Guv Sanjay Malhotra laid out 5 major points around the usage of AI in banking last week at FIBAC 2026.

But all these points, though important, are very basic implementation of AI in finance.

AI, quantum tech can revolutionalise speed of transactions, settlements, completely reimagine banking services.

We are playing very safe with AI, and its important given the complexity of our economy.

But the regulator should open sandbox test cases, encourage startups to build revolutionary tech which can completely re-imagine banking.

Some crystal gazing is required at the policy level, ofcourse within controlled environments.

items.title: The leveraged ETF market is seeing massive inflows. US-listed leveraged ETF market exposure is up to $420 billion, the highest since early July. Over ...
items.description_html:
The leveraged ETF market is seeing massive inflows.

US-listed leveraged ETF market exposure is up to $420 billion, the highest since early July.

Over the last 3 weeks, exposure has surged by more than +$100 billion.

At the same time, assets under management (AUM) have risen +$40 billion, to $180 billion.

The gap between AUM and exposure comes from leverage: a 2x ETF with $100 billion in assets creates $200 billion in market exposure, while a 3x ETF creates $300 billion.

This means the true market impact of leveraged ETFs is nearly 2.5x their headline AUM.

At this pace, both metrics will exceed their June all-time highs as early as next month.

There has never been more leverage in the market.

Chinese integrated circuit industry revenue jumped +22% YoY in 2025, to a record $245 billion.

As a result, China now accounts for ~6% of the global semiconductor market.

This is roughly in-line with Japan and the European Union, at ~7% each, and Taiwan, at ~6%.

By comparison, North America represents 53% of the market, while South Korea accounts for 21%.

China is rapidly emerging as a major global player in semiconductors.

items.title: BREAKING: China's net new loans dropped -$50.4 billion in July, marking only the 3rd monthly decline this century. This is a broad measure of new bank...
items.description_html:
BREAKING: China's net new loans dropped -$50.4 billion in July, marking only the 3rd monthly decline this century.

This is a broad measure of new bank lending in China and a key gauge of overall economic activity.

The decline was also more than 3x larger than expected.

Loans extended specifically to the real economy posted an even sharper drop, with net repayments of -$87.5 billion, the largest monthly decline in data going back to 2002.

Aggregate financing, a broader measure of total credit, rose +$207.7 billion, but almost all of it came from +$192.9 billion in government bond sales rather than organic private lending.

This comes as corporate and household longer-term loans shrank, reflecting weak investment appetite and demand for property.

China's economic activity is deteriorating sharply.

items.title: Markets are bracing for a more volatile period ahead: S&P 500 options are pricing a daily implied move of ~0.75% on August 27th, the day after Nvidia,...
items.description_html:
Markets are bracing for a more volatile period ahead:

S&P 500 options are pricing a daily implied move of ~0.75% on August 27th, the day after Nvidia, $NVDA, reports its quarterly earnings.

The following day, August 28th, carries a ~0.70% implied move in the index as the Jackson Hole symposium begins, making them the two most anticipated volatility events of the month.

By comparison, typical daily implied moves on non-event days this week are just ~0.40-0.50%.

At the same time, options positioning flipped from long to short gamma in early August, a dynamic that tends to amplify market swings once volatility picks up.

Meanwhile, the volatility index, $VIX, finished last week at 14.3 points, the lowest level since December 2025.

More volatility is likely ahead of us.

items.description_html:
China’s Ant Financial is selling about a 5% stake in Paytm, which will be worth over Rs 5,000 crore based on its latest market cap.

Alibaba and Ant had sold all their direct stakes in Paytm by last year.

The latest stake sale will take the total cash realised by Alibaba and Ant to over Rs 21,000 crore

This is against about Rs 7,000 crore invested in Paytm between 2015 and 2020.

Ant will continue to have an economic interest through Resilient Asset Management, whose voting rights are controlled by Paytm founder Vijay Shekhar Sharma.

At one point, Alibaba and Ant directly owned about 40% of Paytm.

After this sale, they will be left with just a 5% indirect economic interest.

items.title: This is unprecedented: 2026 is currently on track to become the only calendar year in at least 30 years with zero 80%+ NYSE downside-volume days. Thes...
items.description_html:
This is unprecedented:

2026 is currently on track to become the only calendar year in at least 30 years with zero 80%+ NYSE downside-volume days.

These are days when at least 80% of NYSE trading volume comes from declining stocks, signaling unusually broad-based selling pressure.

By comparison, 2008 had 49 such days during the Financial Crisis, versus 33 during the 2022 bear market and just 9 last year.

Meanwhile, the average since 1997 is 21 such trading days, with no calendar year ever recording fewer than 5.

In other words, broad-based selling pressure has been almost nonexistent so far in 2026.

The market is more resilient than ever.

items.title: BREAKING: Nvidia, $NVDA, has agreed to provide a more than $100 billion backstop for a massive new OpenAI data center in Ohio, per FT. Details include...
items.description_html:
BREAKING: Nvidia, $NVDA, has agreed to provide a more than $100 billion backstop for a massive new OpenAI data center in Ohio, per FT.

Details include:

1. Nvidia will provide credit support for the "land, power and shell" for the facility capped at $105 billion

2. The data center is being developed alongside a SoftBank-led energy companies

3. Nvidia will also invest $1.5 billion into SB Energy, an energy company founded as part of the SoftBank Group in 2019

items.title: RT Aditi Shrivastava: 🚨🚨 Zepto investor Raamdeo Agrawal called its IPO plans premature after the company deferred its listing. 1️⃣ On when com...
items.description_html:
RT Aditi Shrivastava
🚨🚨 Zepto investor Raamdeo Agrawal called its IPO plans premature after the company deferred its listing.

1️⃣ On when companies should tap the public markets:

“Till companies are actually profitable, or very close to becoming profitable within a visible timeframe, they should not tap the public market. Because it is very difficult to make the public market understand the underlying value.”

2️⃣ On what public-market investors prioritise:

“Earnings, earnings and earnings.”

3️⃣ On why private investors may be more willing to accept losses:

“You could be growing at 100%, and so there will be a cost of acquisition and, hence, there will be some losses. A large private investor can understand that; the public market cannot.”

4️⃣ On Zepto’s IPO timing:

“So my sense is that maybe it was a little premature for the company to tap the public market, and that too at this scale. They must have learnt from this.”

5️⃣ On his personal investment in Zepto:

“Whenever something fails like this, I feel bad. You don't want any entrepreneur to go through this kind of pain. Whether my investment is a failure will be decided after 10 years, not now.”

Source: ET

items.title: RT Exencial Research Partners: Supply Chain stages for rare earth element magnets GEOGRAPHIC FRAGMENTATION OF THE VALUE CHAIN: NO COUNTRY DOMINATES EV...
items.description_html:
RT Exencial Research Partners
Supply Chain stages for rare earth element magnets

GEOGRAPHIC FRAGMENTATION OF THE VALUE CHAIN: NO COUNTRY DOMINATES EVERY LINK

China dominates reserves (34% of global REO-equivalent content), mining (~62% of global output) and, most decisively, refining/separation (91%) and NdFeB magnet manufacturing (92-94%).

Japan's advantage sits almost entirely downstream - in alloy technology and sintered magnet know-how where it holds roughly 6-7% of global magnet capacity but a disproportionate share of automotive-grade process expertise.

India, by contrast, ranks meaningfully only in reserves (world's 3rd or 4th largest, depending on classification) and has negligible mining, ~1% of global refining capacity, and zero commercial magnet manufacturing prior to the current scheme.

items.title: RT Anchit Gupta: This is a very understandable and well-meaning concern, but I think it misses why display flying exists in the first place. For an Ai...
items.description_html:
RT Anchit Gupta
This is a very understandable and well-meaning concern, but I think it misses why display flying exists in the first place.

For an Air Force, attracting high-quality young men and women is a permanent operational requirement. Aircraft, technology and doctrines change, but the institution must continually persuade another generation to choose an unusually demanding profession.

Flying displays have historically been one of the most powerful ways of doing that. In interviews with veterans across generations, I have repeatedly heard versions of the same story: a young boy watched an aircraft display, saw a fighter at close quarters, or encountered the Air Force pilot at an air show, and decided that this was what he wanted to do with his life.

And that is why display teams should not really be viewed simply as “mascots”. They are among an Air Force’s most visible ambassadors. They bring military aviation before people who may otherwise never encounter it, demonstrate precision, discipline, teamwork and professional excellence, and help create the fascination from which future pilots, engineers and airmen emerge. Most major air forces maintain such teams for much the same reason.

The fact that some of the finest pilots are selected is also not incidental. Display flying is extremely demanding, and its credibility rests precisely on the standards of those who perform it. Every possible precaution is taken, but aviation can never be made entirely risk-free. The occasional tragedy, however painful, cannot by itself become the argument for abandoning an activity that has inspired generations to enter the service.

Dhali’s loss was a terrible one. But I would be cautious about framing it as a life lost for an air show. He was performing a recognised professional role within the Air Force, one that has contributed for decades to recruiting, outreach and the public connection with military aviation.

items.title: If you invest in growth stocks, accidents will happen. That is simply part of equity investing. A fast growing company does not necessarily have to ge...
items.description_html:
If you invest in growth stocks, accidents will happen.

That is simply part of equity investing.

A fast growing company does not necessarily have to generate strong cash flows from day one.

During the early stages of growth, a large part of the capital may be getting absorbed into inventory, receivables, capacity expansion.

The important question is not whether cash flow is weak today.

The important question is whether the business is moving towards generating adequate cash flows in the future.

Because growth has to be funded somehow.

If internal cashflows are not sufficient, the company eventually has only two major options - debt or equity.

During a bull market, this may not look like a serious problem. Capital is easily available, valuations are high & companies can raise money through QIPs or other equity issuances without causing too much pain.

The real test comes during a bear market.

When valuations collapse & investors are no longer willing to provide capital, a company that continuously requires external funding can suddenly find itself in a very difficult position.

Its never a good idea to reject every high growth company simply because its current CFO is weak.

If you follow that rule blindly, you will miss a lot of exceptional businesses.

There are several companies where cash flows looked poor during the initial years because almost every rupee was being reinvested into growth. Once the business matured, working capital situation improved, cash generation improved significantly.

Markets usually reward that transition very well.

But the opposite is equally important.

If REV & PAT keep growing year after year while cash flows never improve, working capital keeps stretching, debt keeps increasing or fresh equity is repeatedly required just to sustain the business, eventually something can go wrong.

That is why the trend matters far more than one year's number.

- Is CFO improving relative to EBITDA?
- Are receivable days normalising?
- Is inventory growth broadly in line with business growth?
- Is the company becoming less dependent on external capital?

These are the questions that need to be tracked continuously.

And many times, the warning signs don't appear overnight.

You will often get clues in Cashflow statement & Balance Sheet.

This is why regular tracking is so important.

We were not invested in Zaggle, but I know many investors who have been impacted by the recent fall. Situations like these are also a reminder that no matter how strong the story appears, risk management can never be ignored.

Accidents will happen
You will get some investments wrong
That is normal.

What matters is making sure that one mistake does not damage the portfolio permanently.

This is why I keep emphasising adequate diversification.

For many investors, a portfolio of around 20-25 stocks can be a reasonable starting point, although the right number will always depend on portfolio size, time horizon, risk appetite etc

The objective is not to avoid every mistake
That is impossible.

The objective is to survive the mistakes when they happen.

Because in equity investing, survival comes first.

If you survive long enough, you give yourself the opportunity to learn, improve & eventually thrive.

items.description_html:
*Key Announcements and Focus Areas from PM Modi's 13th consecutive Independence Day Speech (India's 80th)*

1. *Youth and AI Skilling* - Announced a nationwide program to train 1 cr young people in AI skills over the next year and introduced a free online coaching network for competitive examinations

2. *The "Saptadhara" Framework* - Outlined a 7 point economic roadmap focusing on manufacturing, agriculture/food processing, technology/innovation, high-speed connectivity (Gatishakti), defense self-reliance (Aatmanirbhar), green/blue economy, and national soft power

3. *Energy and Nuclear Targets* - Set a long-term goal of achieving 100 GW of nuclear power capacity by 2047, alongside plans to operationalize 5 new nuclear reactors within the decade under the SHANTI Act

4. *Warning on "Dimagi Naxals"* - Cautioned against ideological or intellectual extremism ("dimagi Naxals") in society even as armed left-wing extremism has largely been eradicated

5. *Digital Census and Vision 2047* Urged the youth to actively assist their families in completing a seamless digital census, reiterating the ultimate goal of building a fully developed Viksit Bharat by 2047

6. *Fortune 500 Targets* The government set a goal to have 50 Indian companies listed on the Fortune 500

7. The vision includes *pushing an Indian bank and top pharmaceutical firms into the world's top 5*

8. Businesses were urged to build strong international brands and *expand global footprints in technology, banking, and professional services*

9. *Semiconductors & Manufacturing* Highlighting a push for domestic tech ecosystems, the *plan targets 7–8 new semiconductor plants over the next 1–2 years*

10. Noted India’s transition from the fragile 5 economies to the world's fastest-growing major economy

11. *Trade and MSMEs* MSMEs were encouraged to capitalize on India's expanding network of Free Trade Agreements (FTAs) to scale exports

12. *Tax and Regulatory Relief* A simplified, next-generation GST reform package was teased as an upcoming regulatory ease-of-doing-business measure

items.description_html:
The cost of servicing US debt is the highest in decades:

On Thursday, the US government sold $25 billion of 30Y Treasury bonds at a 5.216% yield, the highest auction yield since 2001.

This follows a $42 billion auction of 10Y Treasury notes on Wednesday that resulted in a 4.683% yield, the highest since 2007.

Previously, on July 9th, the government sold 30Y Treasury bonds at a 5.058% yield, the highest since 2007, highlighting the worsening trend in US debt financing costs.

By comparison, yields on the same-maturity Treasury auctions were below 2.00% during the 2020 pandemic.

This comes as investors are demanding more compensation to finance the US government's ever-growing deficit.

In July, the US Treasury’s budget deficit surged +$141 billion YoY, to $432 billion, the largest July total in history.

The US debt crisis is entering uncharted territory.

US consumers are pulling back on spending:

US retail sales dropped -0.6% in July, the largest monthly decrease since May 2025, missing expectations of a +0.1% increase.

The biggest drop came from non-store retailers, including Amazon, $AMZN, where sales fell -2.2%, the 2nd-largest decline since July 2021.

At the same time, motor vehicle and parts dealer sales fell -1.8%.

As a result, retail sales excluding auto fell -0.3%, below the expected +0.2% increase.

Meanwhile, control-group sales, which feed into the GDP calculation, plunged -0.4%, the largest monthly decline since January 2025.

The measure excludes food services, auto dealers, building materials stores, and gas stations.

Americans are becoming more cautious with their spending.

The top 1% of US businesses spent a record median of $7,400 per employee per month on AI in July, according to Ramp.

This compares to a record $650 per employee for the top 10% of businesses and $11.95 per employee for the median firm.

Over the last several months, AI spend per employee has more than tripled for all these groups.

The surge is widening the gap between categories, with the top 1% now spending more than 600 times as much per employee as the typical company.

To put this into perspective, the top 1% of US businesses were spending less than $1,000 per employee per month on AI in early 2024.

AI investment is becoming increasingly concentrated among a handful of companies.

items.title: Thanks, Sanjeev! Most investing books are written under the illumination of hindsight. Framing Business Uncertainty was never designed to back-test a ...
items.description_html:
Thanks, Sanjeev!

Most investing books are written under the illumination of hindsight. Framing Business Uncertainty was never designed to back-test a thesis or explain an event ex-post.

On p.192, I compared the systems of PI Industries and Laurus Labs using the framework explained in the book and summarised in my pinned X post.

The point was not to predict next year’s earnings. The point was to read the system before the financial statements caught up.

The system should give you a green or red light ex-ante, ideally a few years before the P&L confirms what was already visible in the underlying architecture.

Reported numbers are lagging evidence.

The edge is seeing the system change before the numbers do.

items.title: Results season is over. Now is the time to step back & look at every company in the portfolio on a holistic basis. During the quarter, the focus is na...
items.description_html:
Results season is over.

Now is the time to step back & look at every company in the portfolio on a holistic basis.

During the quarter, the focus is naturally on results - who beat expectations, who disappointed & whether the rate of change is improving.

But once the noise settles, every company in the portfolio needs to be looked at again from a much broader perspective.

The starting point is simple - what were we expecting from the business before the quarter, and what has actually changed after the results?

Just because a stock has worked well for us in the past does not mean it deserves to remain in the portfolio forever. Similarly, being down on a position is not a reason to continue holding it if the original assumptions have changed.

The business should earn its place in the portfolio every quarter.

The business has to be evaluated as it stands today.

At the portfolio level, one of the most important things I look at is earnings growth.

Ideally, portfolio level EPS growth should remain above 20%.

Over shorter periods, stock prices can move because of liquidity, narratives etc. But over longer periods, earnings remain one of the strongest drivers of returns.

Allocation is equally important.

Conviction should not remain static.

If a company continues to execute well, earnings visibility improves and the outlook becomes stronger, the allocation can be reassessed accordingly.

On the other hand, if growth is slowing, execution is deteriorating or the original thesis is no longer playing out, there should be no hesitation in reducing exposure.

At the same time, diversification remains extremely important.

No matter how high the conviction, a portfolio should not become excessively dependent on a single company or a particular sector.

Unexpected accidents - regulatory changes, governance issues, industry disruptions or company specific execution problems - are far more common than we assume.

Good portfolio construction is not only about finding the right companies.

It is also about ensuring that one wrong decision does not have a disproportionate impact on the overall portfolio.

Results season gives us a fresh set of information.

Now is the time to process it properly - revisit every thesis, reset expectations, change allocations wherever required and explore new opportunities where the earnings trajectory and rate of change are improving.

The aim should be simple:

Enter the next results season with a portfolio that is fundamentally stronger than the one with which we entered this one.

items.title: ▶️More than four million hectares of protected tropical forest — an area twice the size of Wales — has been destroyed by wildfires since 2001, acc...
items.description_html:
▶️More than four million hectares of protected tropical forest — an area twice the size of Wales — has been destroyed by wildfires since 2001, according to the most detailed global assessment of its kind.

▶️The vast majority of the destruction — around 89 per cent — occurred in the tropical Americas, particularly in Brazil.

▶️The rate of destruction inside protected areas is around nine times higher since 2016.

▶️Protected status does reduce the chances of wildfires in most of the regions studied, but does not shield forests from the worldwide trend of worsening wildfire activity.

▶️Researchers from the University of Sheffield say protected area planning must now factor in future wildfire risk if these measures are to remain effective as the impact of climate change intensifies.

https://www.downtoearth.org.in/natural-disasters/wildfires-have-destroyed-an-area-of-protected-tropical-forest-twice-the-size-of-wales-globally-since-2001-study-reveals

🔽 Below: A dead caiman in the Brazilian Pantanal after wildfires struck the region in 2020.

items.title: 👉The critically endangered Great Indian Bustard (GIB) has vanished from most of the Indian Subcontinent, especially the Deccan Plateau. But it has ...
items.description_html:
👉The critically endangered Great Indian Bustard (GIB) has vanished from most of the Indian Subcontinent, especially the Deccan Plateau. But it has a chance of making a comeback there, provided traditional agriculture and land use are resorted to, according to a new study.

👉 @wildwithwolves, @shaheerkhan and Gautam Talukdar found that approximately 48,000 km2 (6.6%) of the total land area of the Deccan landscape is suitable for GIB. This is distributed across 35 districts (22 in Maharashtra, six in Karnataka and Telangana, and one in Andhra Pradesh).

👉Priority conservation areas from different regions of the Deccan landscape were identified, ranging from 144-8496 km2 at 16 sites by using landscape-level surveys and distribution modelling.

👉Khan, Talukdar and Habib note that promoting traditional, low-intensity land-use practices can further enhance habitat suitability and support the species’ ecological requirements in the Deccan.

https://www.downtoearth.org.in/wildlife-biodiversity/can-the-great-indian-bustard-reclaim-the-deccan-part-of-its-range-yes-provided-traditional-agriculture-is-promoted-says-study

They can attract investors settled abroad (financially well-to-do) to participate in the stock markets with relative ease.

I had written for ET in July how the industry was suffering from slowdown because of traditional paper-based KYC mechanisms followed in this sector.

There are more than 900K NRI accounts opened till May 2026 but the assets held in these accounts were at Rs 6 lakh crore.

This value was growing at the slowest pace in recent times.

Now with KYC getting simplified and more brokers scaling up onboarding, perhaps this will change.

items.title: Consumer confidence is rapidly declining in the US. The 6-month average of the Consumer Confidence Index for Generation X is down to ~78 points, the l...
items.description_html:
Consumer confidence is rapidly declining in the US.

The 6-month average of the Consumer Confidence Index for Generation X is down to ~78 points, the lowest in at least 5 years.

At the same time, this metric for Baby Boomers is down to ~80 points, the lowest since at least September 2021.

By comparison, readings for both age groups stood at ~110 points in October 2021, or ~40% higher.

Meanwhile, the Silent Generation's Consumer Confidence Index has fallen in 5 months of 2026, to ~81 points, the lowest in at least 5 years.

The gauge remains above 100 points only for Generation Z and Millennials, but even those readings are still below their 2021-2023 levels.

Consumer confidence remains well below post-pandemic highs across every generation.

RT Savitri Mumukshu - सावित्री मुमुक्षु
In 1939 under the Nizam, Hyderabad's Osmania University and schools expelled 1200 Hindu students for daring to sing Vande Mataram in the Hindu prayer hall on Janamashtami day. The Hindu prayer hall was then locked up and students were served with an order prohibiting them from singing the song within University precincts. They were then forced to either write an apology or be rusticated. The Education Department had issued an official order prohibiting singing of Vande Mataram in all schools in Hyderabad. Consequently 1200 of the Hindu students who dared to stand up for the national song were forcibly expelled and had their academic careers destroyed.

In the same Osmania university when Muslim students were celebrating Milad-al-Nabi, the presiding Professor said " I am pained to see the inertness amongst the Muslims, when there STILL exist 22 crores of Gobar-Parast (dung worshippers)"!

Millions of patriots fought so hard for the right to sing the complete version of Vande Mātaram which expresses the soul of Bharat Mata. And yet today we have Neo-Nizams who get heartburn when we sing the full version of our national song even in Independent India!

Source: Munshi, Kanaiyalal Maneklal. The End of an Era; Hyderabad Memories. India, Bharatiya Vidya Bhavan, 1957.

items.title: RT Not Just Headlines: 🚨India’s First Private Nuclear Fusion Tokamak Is Now on the Floor: A Tiny Bengaluru Startup Steps Into the Race to Harness ...
items.description_html:
RT Not Just Headlines
🚨India’s First Private Nuclear Fusion Tokamak Is Now on the Floor: A Tiny Bengaluru Startup Steps Into the Race to Harness the Power of the Sun

India’s nuclear journey has entered a new phase. A Bengaluru-based startup, Pranos Fusion Energy, has built PRAJNA, reportedly India’s first privately developed tokamak for nuclear-fusion research.

Unlike conventional fission, which splits atoms, fusion attempts to replicate the process powering the Sun, combining light atomic nuclei under extreme conditions to release enormous energy.

PRAJNA is a remarkably compact spherical tokamak, with a reported major radius of around 0.4 metres. It is not designed to generate commercial electricity yet. Instead, it serves as a test bed for experimenting with plasma confinement, magnetic systems and other technologies needed for future fusion reactors.

That approach could be strategically important. While giant fusion projects such as ITER require enormous infrastructure and decades of research, compact tokamaks can potentially be built, modified and tested faster and at lower cost.

The breakthrough is particularly significant because India's fusion programme has historically been dominated by government institutions, especially the Institute for Plasma Research under the Department of Atomic Energy. India already has substantial experience in tokamak research, including the SST-1 programme and experiments involving extremely high-temperature plasma.

Now, India's private sector is entering the field.

PRAJNA does not mean India has solved commercial fusion. Sustaining stable plasma, achieving net energy gain and eventually producing economical electricity remain enormous scientific and engineering challenges.

But the direction is unmistakable.

As the US, China, Europe, Japan, South Korea and others race to unlock practical fusion, India is building its own capabilities through both government research and private innovation.

The machine may be tiny.

The ambition behind it is anything but.

items.description_html:
Titan - Interesting Insights on Cash for Gold & Gold Exchange

Titan rolled out Cash for Gold across all stores from June

Under this initiative, customers can bring their old gold to Titan & receive cash instead of necessarily exchanging it for new jewellery

Titan does not primarily view Cash for Gold as a new REV stream

The philosophy is more around solving a customer problem, widening the basket of services offered by Tanishq & potentially bringing new customers into the ecosystem

Exchange has already become a very important growth and customer acquisition engine for Titan.

Management: "...exchange continues to be a big driver of customer acquisition & a big driver of growth for us."

Sales linked to exchange - including old gold purchased elsewhere as well as gold originally bought from Tanishq - now contribute more than 50% of the jewellery business.

A similar trend is being witnessed across other jewellery companies

Kalyan Jewellers - Recycled gold contributed more than 46% of Q1 REV & crossed 55% in June.

Management aims to sustain recycled gold at 55-60% of REV, which should structurally reduce dependence on imported gold

Higher old gold exchange temporarily diluted margins by around 20-30 bps during the quarter

However, Kalyan is simultaneously scaling its Cash for Gold business, where gold is purchased below the prevailing spot price

This business is margin accretive & can partly offset the dilution arising from higher exchange transactions

Overall, recycled gold is increasingly becoming an important sourcing, customer acquisition & working capital lever for organised jewellery players

items.title: Xinhua: "China's yuan-denominated loans rose by 10.38 trillion yuan in the first seven months of 2026, with outstanding yuan loans up 5.1 percent year...
items.description_html:
Xinhua: "China's yuan-denominated loans rose by 10.38 trillion yuan in the first seven months of 2026, with outstanding yuan loans up 5.1 percent year on year, according to the People's Bank of China."

What Xinhua chose not to mention in its article, but what nearly everyone else will focus on, is that Chinese banks recorded a net decline of 340 billion yuan in new yuan loans in July, well below already-low expectations for a 120-130 billion increase.

But while the sharp and unexpected decline in lending in July will get most of the attention from analysts and the press, what is much more important to me is that total social financing, the best proxy for total debt, actually grew quite strongly in July, by 1.4 trillion yuan.

This highlights what we have been seeing all year, which is that China's financing activity is undergoing a structural shift, with the economy relying more than ever on state-led borrowing – and less than ever on private-sector borrowing – to support growth.
https://english.news.cn/20260814/68d17a9cd8294f23b2b170096e688f02/c.html

items.title: Li Wei, associate dean at Cheung Kong Graduate School of Business, writes in Caixin that "to genuinely reduce its trade surplus, China must either inc...
items.description_html:
Li Wei, associate dean at Cheung Kong Graduate School of Business, writes in Caixin that "to genuinely reduce its trade surplus, China must either increase investment or boost domestic consumption. With the marginal returns on traditional infrastructure and real estate investment severely diminished, the only sustainable path is to increase household consumption. This requires profound structural reform. The ultimate goal of such reform is to transfer wealth and income share from the state and corporate sectors to households."

This is increasingly becoming how most Chinese economists understand the Chinese economy, although only recently have they been so public about it. The key point here (and one with which many Chinese economists still disagree) is that with marginal returns on most investment so low, reducing China's trade surplus through an increase in investment will only make the longer-term adjustment worse.

China, in other words, should be reducing investment, not raising it, in order to regain control over misallocated capital and surging debt, but this also means that the only way to rebalance domestically and reduce the trade surplus requires that saving declines even faster.

Li Wei lists one of the ways the saving share of GDP can decline, by transferring income share from the state and corporate sectors to households in order to boost consumption growth relative to the growth in production.

He is right, of course. This is certainly one way to reduce saving and bring the trade surplus down, but it won't be easy because doing so will undermine China's manufacturing competitiveness.

Unfortunately, there is only one other alternative, and it is much worse. The reduction in saving can also occur with a sharp fall in production growth. As production declines faster that consumption, the saving share automatically declines.

Historically this has been how most countries with a similar problem have been forced to adjust, mainly because, like China, they postponed boosting consumption growth for far too long and instead doubled down on their high-investment-growth model.

Beijing, of course, will want to do everything it can to avoid this form of adjustment, but the longer it postpones adjustment by boosting consumption growth, the more likely the Chinese economy will adjust through a fall in production growth.
https://www.caixinglobal.com/2026-08-14/commentary-the-phantom-menace-of-chinese-overcapacity-102474051.html

items.title: RT Jesús Fernández-Villaverde: A young person asked me today for a few papers that would be great to read early on in one’s career. Here is a list ...
items.description_html:
RT Jesús Fernández-Villaverde
A young person asked me today for a few papers that would be great to read early on in one’s career. Here is a list I came up with (I posted a shorter list earlier in reply to a comment). There are many other great papers (and I apologize if I didn’t include yours), but my goal was to focus on papers that a 21-year-old undergrad would enjoy a lot. A paper on the asymptotic properties of the bootstrap or on some subtle point about New Keynesian models, as important as it might be, is not what I am looking for. Also, of course, the list reflects my deeply biased taste. So, feel free to add in the comment section other papers you love!

Philippe Aghion and Peter Howitt (1992), “A Model of Growth Through Creative Destruction,” Econometrica.

George A. Akerlof (1970), “The Market for ‘Lemons’: Quality Uncertainty and the Market Mechanism,” Quarterly Journal of Economics.

Armen A. Alchian (1950), “Uncertainty, Evolution, and Economic Theory,” Journal of Political Economy.

William J. Baumol (1967), “Macroeconomics of Unbalanced Growth: The Anatomy of Urban Crisis,” American Economic Review.

Gary S. Becker (1973), “A Theory of Marriage: Part I,” Journal of Political Economy.

Douglas W. Diamond and Philip H. Dybvig (1983), “Bank Runs, Deposit Insurance, and Liquidity,” Journal of Political Economy.

Xavier Gabaix (1999), “Zipf’s Law for Cities: An Explanation,” Quarterly Journal of Economics.

Xavier Gabaix and Augustin Landier (2008), “Why Has CEO Pay Increased So Much?,” Quarterly Journal of Economics.

Luis Garicano (2000), “Hierarchies and the Organization of Knowledge in Production,” Journal of Political Economy.

Edward L. Glaeser, Bruce Sacerdote and José A. Scheinkman (1996), “Crime and Social Interactions,” Quarterly Journal of Economics.

Sanford J. Grossman and Joseph E. Stiglitz (1980), “On the Impossibility of Informationally Efficient Markets,” American Economic Review.

Oliver Hart and John Moore (1990), “Property Rights and the Nature of the Firm,” Journal of Political Economy.

Friedrich A. Hayek (1945), “The Use of Knowledge in Society, American Economic Review.

Bengt Holmström (1979), “Moral Hazard and Observability,” Bell Journal of Economics.

Charles I. Jones (1995), “R&D-Based Models of Economic Growth,” Journal of Political Economy.

Charles I. Jones (2005), “The Shape of Production Functions and the Direction of Technical Change,” Quarterly Journal of Economics.

Michael Kremer (1993), “Population Growth and Technological Change: One Million B.C. to 1990,” Quarterly Journal of Economics.

Michael Kremer (1993), “The O-Ring Theory of Economic Development,” Quarterly Journal of Economics.

Paul Krugman (1991), “Increasing Returns and Economic Geography,” Journal of Political Economy.

Robert E. Lucas, Jr. (1978), “On the Size Distribution of Business Firms,” Bell Journal of Economics.

Kevin M. Murphy, Andrei Shleifer and Robert W. Vishny (1989), “Industrialization and the Big Push,” Journal of Political Economy.

Paul M. Romer (1990), “Endogenous Technological Change,” Journal of Political Economy.

Sherwin Rosen (1981), “The Economics of Superstars,” American Economic Review.

Alvin E. Roth (2007), “Repugnance as a Constraint on Markets,” Journal of Economic Perspectives.

Thomas C. Schelling (1971), “Dynamic Models of Segregation,” Journal of Mathematical Sociology.

Andrei Shleifer and Robert W. Vishny (1993), “Corruption,” Quarterly Journal of Economics.

Michael Spence (1973), “Job Market Signaling,” Quarterly Journal of Economics.

Robert M. Townsend (1979), “Optimal Contracts and Competitive Markets with Costly State Verification,” Journal of Economic Theory.

Martin L. Weitzman (1974), “Prices vs. Quantities,” Review of Economic Studies.

items.title: RT Jesús Fernández-Villaverde: Sometimes, when I want to lift my spirits, as this week after brooding about the state of much of academia, I want to...
items.description_html:
RT Jesús Fernández-Villaverde
Sometimes, when I want to lift my spirits, as this week after brooding about the state of much of academia, I want to read a great paper I have already read dozens of times. Those are the papers that inspired me as a younger scholar and that, even today, make me slightly jealous.

One of my favorite go-tos is “The O-Ring Theory of Economic Development,” by the inimitable Michael Kremer, at UChicago Econ.

The idea is that producing output requires many tasks, and failure in just one of them drastically lowers the value of the final output. My favorite examples are the British cars of the 1950s and early 1960s. Think of the Jaguars or the Austin-Healeys. Was anything ever more gorgeous than an XK120 in British Racing Green? And yet, that Moss gearbox with no synchro on first! Go for a Porsche 356 if you have the money, because the Jaguar will eventually break your heart.

But the paper is gorgeous because Kremer takes this simple observation and builds a whole theory of differences in output across countries around it. He lets the quality of each task multiply rather than add up, as in standard models. A good worker is worth more next to other good workers, so the best end up working with the best and wages fan out. And a small difference in the chance of a mistake, compounded over dozens of tasks, becomes a huge difference in output per worker across countries, plus a large set of predictions about the distribution of firms, wage correlations, matching, and more.

Here, back in 2014:

https://nadaesgratis.es/fernandez-villaverde/las-juntas-t%c3%b3ricas-de-espa%c3%b1a

I used that model to think about some of Spain’s economic problems (an automatic translator will give you a very good English version).

It is such a wonderful and deft piece of economic craftsmanship. Read it. I just did.

items.title: TD Power Systems Limited ("TDPS") has entered into a Build-to-Print Manufacturing Framework Agreement dated August 13, 2026 with Siemens Energy, Inc. ...
items.description_html:
TD Power Systems Limited ("TDPS") has entered
into a Build-to-Print Manufacturing Framework Agreement dated August 13, 2026 with Siemens
Energy, Inc. ("Siemens Energy"), pursuant to which TDPS will manufacture and supply 2-pole
Generators in accordance with Siemens Energy's designs, drawings and specifications.

In simple words

TD Power has signed a 10 year deal with Siemens Energy's US arm to build large 2-pole generators for Siemens.

Siemens gives the designs and drawings, TDPS manufactures them. Siemens is doing this because its own factories are full (the AI data-centre power boom has its order books stuffed for years), so it needs someone qualified to make machines on its behalf.

TDPS has licensed Siemens' 2-pole technology for over a decade, so this is that relationship getting upgraded from "we borrow your design" to "we are your factory."

Business only comes through individual purchase orders whenever Siemens issues them. So nothing goes into the order book today, and since these machines take 18–20 months to build, real revenue starts showing up around FY29.

Also, since TDPS is building to Siemens' design and not its own, it doesn't own the technology and likely earns a thinner margin per unit but with far higher volume, less design risk and better factory utilisation.

Think of it as TDPS becoming a "CDMO for generators" for one of the world's top three turbine makers: strategically a very strong position, but for now it's a licence to receive orders, not the orders themselves.

Disclaimer: No recommendation to buy or sell.

A very interesting company because it has built 15913 cr of revenue in a flash – Just 8 years - without owning most of its factories. It has 6,979 empanelled suppliers across 26 countries on the platform, and roughly 26 owned facilities in 4 countries

The product range is across the spectrum of Industries – From solar modules to wearables, hearables, power equipment, aerospace, defence, metals, and AI infrastructure.

It works with the likes of Siemens Gamesa, Acer India, NextPower, CG Power, NTPC Renewable Energy, L&T, DRDO, NALCO, IOCL, Mortenson, Indian Air Force.
And 80%+ of manufacturing revenue comes from repeat customers.

India’s manufacturing story isn’t just about building more factories. It’s also about building the network that connects them. Zetwerk is building that network. That's what makes the model fascinating.

For years, we have talked about China+1, Make in India, defence indigenisation, renewable energy, and the AI infrastructure capex wave.

It is a great manufacturing play, unlike a traditional manufacturer with one factory making one category of products.

items.title: Garware Hi Tech Films - Q1FY27 Insights REV increased 28% YoY to 633 Cr & PAT increased 60% to 133 Cr Management: "...we do not view this as a result ...
items.description_html:
Garware Hi Tech Films - Q1FY27 Insights

REV increased 28% YoY to 633 Cr & PAT increased 60% to 133 Cr

Management: "...we do not view this as a result of one exceptional quarter. Rather, it reflects the structural transformation of our business over many years."

The margin expansion was driven primarily by specialty product mix, higher end Sun Control Films & the increasing contribution of architectural products

Architectural films are probably becoming one of the most important pieces of the Garware story

Management summed up the philosophy well: "...we do not want to do like a commoditized Sun Control."

The strategy is increasingly to move towards products where performance & technology matter more than price

Management even indicated that 27-28% EBITDA margins appear logical if operating conditions remain supportive, although official FY27 guidance remains at 25% +/- 2%

The D2C transformation is probably the biggest structural change underway

Garware Application Studios have already crossed 250 locations in India, while 14 international studios are operational across the Middle East & US. Garware Home Solutions currently has 9 studios and is targeted to reach 50 by FY27 end

Garware Home Solutions is a 100% D2C model

Management believes that simply taking market share from competitors would eventually limit growth. To reach 3,500 Cr and beyond, it wants to create entirely new use cases & consumer demand

TPU is another major growth & margin trigger

The new TPU facility remains on track for commissioning in Q3FY27

Around 75% of its initial production is expected to be consumed internally for PPF, creating backward integration, while around 25% has been earmarked for newer TPU based specialty products

Management expects the backward integration itself to add around 1.5-2% to margins in FY28

Management believes TPU related products could become a 500 Cr+ business over a 3 year period

When management was asked which new product could become the largest meaningful contributor over the next few years, the answer was straightforward: "...that would be definitely TPU."

Garware is investing around 192 Cr in a highly automated new SCF line with approximately 1,200 lakh sq ft of annual capacity. Commercial production is expected in H1FY28.

Management est potential peak REV from this line at around 500-550 Cr.

Management has reaffirmed FY27 guidance of more than 2,500 Cr REV.

Over the medium term, it continues to target 15-20% REV CAGR. Management also indicated that around 3,500 Cr REV is achievable over the next few years.

What makes Garware particularly interesting is that multiple structural changes are happening simultaneously.

A solar boom has transformed India's power dynamics.

“There is excess energy many a times during the day and the power cost goes down to 1 rupee and in some hours to zero,” Tata Power CEO Praveer Sinha says to me on Bloomberg’s Emerging vodcast.

Late evenings are another story.

Solar generation disappears just as demand remains high. Meeting even 250 GW then is a stretch, says Mohit Bhargava, country director of the India Energy & Climate Center at the University of California, Berkeley. “We had literally every horse running at that point of time,” he says, referring to a continuing reliance on coal-based power.

How electrification, climate change and AI are testing the country’s energy infrastructure.

items.description_html:
RT Amit Puri
Paper worth reading on agentic AI governance by @srajagopalan.

TL;DR:

The paper argues that the key question isn’t whether AI should have legal personhood, but who ultimately bears responsibility when an autonomous agent acts.

Its core idea is that AI governance should focus on identity, authorization, traceability, financial responsibility, and the ability to revoke an agent’s authority. In other words, don’t make the machine responsible but make its agency traceable to someone who is responsible.

This feels increasingly important as AI shifts from generating information to actually taking actions in the economy.

items.title: Centum Electronics is an example of a SELF help story where past poor capital allocation is being fixed by shutting/hiving off Canadian & French Subsi...
items.description_html:
Centum Electronics is an example of a SELF help story where past poor capital allocation is being fixed by shutting/hiving off Canadian & French Subsidiary.

What is a self help story?

1. When a business tries to develop alternate business segments. Often few bets won't go right.

2. Eventually, the ROCE takes a hit as the segments that aren't performing drag the overall performance & return ratios.

3. Over the years, management ends up realising this. And stats fixing the mistakes of poor capital allocation in the past.

This is what we call a Self Help story when this happens

Disc: no reco to buy or sell.

items.description_html:
RT Séb Krier
I highly recommend reading this excellent paper by @srajagopalan, which is the closest to my own thinking on this question.

"Agentic AI makes complex and consequential action possible without continuous human control. Whether the agent should be a legal person then becomes secondary to a prior question: how law allocates responsibility when action is generated without a legally constituted actor to carry it."

Ultimately you always want a human (or human governed entity) to be the beneficial owner that bears the liability; trying to push this onto an agent creates a moral hazard. Legal personality could potentially be functionally useful, but registration, assets, and revocability should always trace back to a human.

https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=7127038

items.title: Wrote this in India Edition not long ago... How did it come to this? When he died two years ago, Ratan Tata left behind three competing power centers ...
items.description_html:
Wrote this in India Edition not long ago...

How did it come to this?

When he died two years ago, Ratan Tata left behind three competing power centers in charge of the group’s principal investment holding company Tata Sons and its owner Tata Trusts, which hold a 66% share.

Homegrown leader Natarajan Chandrasekaran was CEO of the group’s most valuable company, TCS, before being appointed chairman of Tata Sons in 2017.

Noel Tata is Ratan’s estranged half-brother, who’s waited in the shadows for his turn to lead the group. He took over as chairman of Tata Trusts in October 2024 and serves as nominee director on Tata Sons’ board.

Other dramatis personae include Ratan’s friends, such as industrialist Venu Srinivasan, retired bureaucrat Vijay Singh and long-time confidant Mehli Mistry – who are either directors of Tata Sons or trustees of Tata Trusts, or in Srinivasan’s case, both.

Maybe Ratan hoped their differences would serve as checks on any individual power grab or thought he had more time to make allies of them all. Instead, the infighting has gotten so bad it’s tough to tell sides anymore.

https://www.bloomberg.com/news/newsletters/2026-05-07/india-s-tata-group-faces-volatile-future-as-possible-ipo-power-struggles-loom

items.title: RT Ira Dugal: This Bank of America investment in Jio Credit is a big one. For many reasons. The institutions, yes, but also an interesting turn in the...
items.description_html:
RT Ira Dugal
This Bank of America investment in Jio Credit is a big one. For many reasons. The institutions, yes, but also an interesting turn in the history of the Indian financial sector.

Bear with me.

After a burst of expansion in the early 2000s, most American and European lenders retreated from India — partly because of their own mistakes (Citi Financial, HSBC’s micro finance play, Standard Chartered’s corporate mishaps) and partly because tighter global capital rules post the GFC.

India then went through its own credit boom and bust cycle. It’s now back in what I would call a ‘controlled boom’, with credit growing without chunk risks and chunky delinquencies in check.

This has brought back foreign lenders. HSBC chose to go back on its own (partly because it has an Indian banking veteran at the top), Japanese banks came in with big bank and non bank investments(Yes Bank and Shriram), as did Emirates. Fairfax is waiting in the wings with a potential IDBI deal.

And now Bank of America does a Jv with Jio Credit which has recently stepped up growth.

The big difference is that most foreign institutions are now coming in via JVs, banking on crucial local expertise in lending. Building from scratch is no longer viable in a mature Indian market.

Actually if you go far back enough, JVs were the original way that foreign financial institutions came into India (think Kotak - Goldman, Merrill lynch - DSP, Insurance JVs) . But the mood had then turned to full direct play, which didn’t work for most and now back to JVs.

So full circle…

items.description_html:
RT menaka doshi
Tata Group Has a Succession Problem...Again

Be careful what you ask for, they say. It may come true.

Well, with N Chandrasekaran eschewing another term as Tata Sons chairman, Noel Tata seems to have succeeded in consolidating control.

But now Noel faces a fractured board that has to find Chandra's successor while navigating a host of other challenges. For instance, significant capital commitments to new ventures in electronics, aviation, semiconductors, energy and e-commerce businesses.

Besides, as chairman of Tata Trusts, Noel has to ensure all this infighting doesn't expose the trusts to more government intervention.

If he has wrested the crown then he should remember -- uneasy lies the head that wears it.

Read India Edition Daily

items.title: RT Peterson Institute: If Trump's tariffs on other countries end up too high compared with those on China, some supply chains that moved out of China ...
items.description_html:
RT Peterson Institute
If Trump's tariffs on other countries end up too high compared with those on China, some supply chains that moved out of China in the past year might find it advantageous to move back.
💡Lessons from Trump's 2025 tariffs on imports of phones vs. clothing from India & China:
📱In 2025, Trump imposed tariffs on smartphones from China but not India (figure 1 below).
🍎Apple responded to those tariffs on China by quickly sourcing iPhones from India.
📵Those smartphone tariffs were not universal. On Liberation Day, smartphones were exempted from those tariffs.
🍎This exemption incentivized Apple to maintain its sourcing switch away from China. Even when Trump increased overall tariffs on India to 50% in August 2025, he continued to exempt smartphones assembled in India.
📱iPhones assembled in China faced a 20% tariff that iPhones assembled in India did not.
📊Total US imports of smartphones in 2025 did not fall dramatically (figure 2 below).
📈By May 2025, nearly 2/3 of US smartphone imports were arriving from India, up from only 6% as late as October of 2024.
📱Between April 2025-February 2026, nearly half of US smartphone imports were from India.
💡Meanwhile...
👕In 2025, Trump imposed high tariffs on clothing from both China & India.
👖Trump's tariffs on India (both Liberation Day & August) did not exempt clothing.
👚US imports of clothing did not suddenly switch to India (Figure 3 below).
🧦By October 2025, US tariffs on clothing from India were higher than on clothing from China (Figure 4 below).
👗By the end of 2025, the US tariff differential between China & countries like Vietnam & Bangladesh was basically unchanged from pre-Trump 2.0 levels (Figure 4 again).
🧤For clothing, there was little new tariff incentive in 2025 to move a supply chain out of China to alternative destinations (see Figure 3 panel b).
💡Since the IEEPA decision...
➡️US import sourcing for smartphones & clothing has stabilized, but not yet changed dramatically, in response to the major US tariff adjustments beginning in February 2026.
💡Why Trump's next tariff moves could change the dynamics
3⃣0⃣1⃣: A new set of tariffs on 16 countries from ongoing Section 301 investigations into "excess capacity" may increase the tariff differential on imports from China relative to other key foreign suppliers...
...which could incentivize companies to find sources outside of China.
‼️OR Trump's new tariffs could incentivize US imports of certain products to move back to China.
❓Why?
🤔Suppose those upcoming Section 301 tariffs do not result in a significantly wide tariff differential favoring alternative sources, such as India.
‼️If a US company's competitors all source from China & the US tariff on alternative source countries remains too high, the desire to stay in business may force a company to buy from China too.
⚖️Especially if those 301 tariffs are more legally durable than the IEEPA tariffs, the reduction in uncertainty could convince companies to increase their import sourcing from China.
💡For the supply chain implications resulting from Trump's next tariffs & his Board of Trade...
...look for the size of product-level US tariff differentials between China & other major potential source countries.

items.title: Why Increasing Value Per kit important in Auto Ancs? 1. For decades, ancillary revenue was hostage to vehicle volumes. Every auto slowdown hit supplie...
items.description_html:
Why Increasing Value Per kit important in Auto Ancs?

1. For decades, ancillary revenue was hostage to vehicle volumes. Every auto slowdown hit suppliers directly. Content per vehicle breaks that link. Revenue starts compounding independent of how many cars a country actually sells.

2. The EV transition was supposed to be the industry's biggest risk. Single component suppliers tied to fuel systems, exhausts, and ICE only parts face real extinction risk. Suppliers building powertrain agnostic systems across plastics, mechatronics, and structures face none.

3. The scoreboard has changed. It's no longer how many units you sold. It's how much wallet share you own inside every vehicle that rolls off the line. That's the real KPI now.

4. This decouples ancillary earnings from the entire EV debate. Whether a market hits 20% EV penetration or 60% by 2030 stops being the question that decides who wins.

This is why Kit value per vehicle is the key metric to track in Auto Ancs going forward.

Its not about how many clients you have but how much more can you sell to the existing client

Disc: no recommendation to buy or sell. Mental models for different sectors.

items.description_html:
RT ANI
#WATCH | Delhi: On the impact of the US tariff bill on the Indian economy, Chief Rating Officer at CareEdge Ratings, Sachin Gupta, says, “It will have a multi-order impact on the Indian economy. First of all, we have yet to see how the US implements it, because there is a lot of back-and-forth that happens with many of these US regulations. But assuming that there is indeed a 100% tariff levied, we can analyse this impact at two or three levels. One is the most direct impact, which will be on US imports or Indian exports…if there is indeed a 100% tariff, it becomes unviable…if Russian crude oil supply is excluded from the overall global crude market, where total global crude demand is around 100 million barrels a day, with the Strait of Hormuz accounting for 20 million barrels and Russia accounting for about 9 million barrels, of which India and China take roughly 75% and if both India and China decide not to import from Russia at all due to these 100% tariffs, removing up to 30% of global supply will cause a significant impact. While crude prices have recently been relatively benign at around $70 to $85 a barrel, if this scenario becomes a reality, prices could easily go beyond $100 or even $110 to $120 a barrel, causing India's current account deficit to easily more than double from last year's levels strictly on account of crude. Furthermore, at $110 to $120 a barrel, the government would have to pass on those price rises to the fuel pumps, creating a secondary inflationary impact across the broader economy…”

This was the fourth straight quarter of 30%+ EBITDA margins and management expects a further 100-150 bps upside as captive power comes online in Q4.

The order book is tilting toward export industrials and PV. A ₹950 crore peak annual revenue pipeline and mostly export-oriented industrial and passenger-vehicle programs is already ramping up and will reshape the revenue mix over the next 2-3 years.

Management is guiding for high-teens volume growth. A new product stream (250 kg to 3-ton parts) starts contributing from Q3/Q4 FY28-29 onwards.

items.description_html:
🚨 C2C’s auditor has issued a qualified opinion and flagged multiple serious financial and compliance concerns:

1️⃣ Liquidity & Going Concern Risk:
The company is facing a liquidity crisis, with statutory dues unpaid due to lack of funds. Recovery from trade receivables remains uncertain, while operations are heavily dependent on short-term promoter funding. The auditor has raised doubt over C2C’s ability to continue as a going concern. Liquidation Risk

2️⃣ CSR Payments Not Cleared:
CSR expenses were recognised through cheques, creating a book overdraft. However, the cheques were not presented for payment. The auditor noted that the CSR obligation is discharged only when the payment is actually cleared.

3️⃣ Statutory Dues Pending:
Undisputed statutory payments remain unpaid. No provision has been made for possible interest or penalties. Delays in filing statutory returns and weak internal controls were also highlighted.

4️⃣ Labour Code Impact Not Assessed:
The company has not quantified the potential impact of new labour regulations on gratuity, provident fund, wages and other employee benefits.

5️⃣ FEMA Compliance Issues:
Overseas receivables remain unrealised beyond RBI timelines. Applications for regularisation are pending, SOFTEX registration is yet to be approved, and possible penalties have not been provided for.

items.title: We initiated Sansera for our subscribers around 16th December 2025. But the more important thing is how we filtered on this idea. > First key factor w...
items.description_html:
We initiated Sansera for our subscribers around 16th December 2025.

But the more important thing is how we filtered on this idea.

> First key factor we observed was the product mix change, where the company's intent was to gradually move from its ICE component business to Aero/Defence/Semicon (ADS) business.

> This product mix shift was visible from the fact that margins had been improving over the last 2 quarters, and growth was starting to pick up. That's how it came under our filters.

> Going a little deeper, we understood that the kind of things it was doing in the ADS business were quite moated. It had a single-source monopoly on Airbus A350/A320 thrust-reversal gimbals with zero defects over 12 years; hogging (machining from solid billet vs. forging) is a much harder-to-replicate capability for aerospace tolerances.

> Also, in its semiconductor business, it was working with Lam Research, where this year their business is expected to go from $10M to $30M .

> Also, as per our channel checks, they had orders/interest from Rolls-Royce for aero-engine feelers, the MMRFIC JV (navy fuses, radars), and a Tesla ESS order.

> All these things were a confirmation of our thesis that management has the capabilities, and that the product mix is changing for good.

> They have also given strong guidance of ₹8,000 Cr in revenue, with ADS at 20–25% of overall business and blended EBITDA margins moving above the 20% mark.

On top of this, we also visited their facility, where we got to understand the manufacturing complexity involved in the components they make for their ADS business, and their capabilities in precision engineering.

The framework was simple: through scanning, found a business where earnings were breaking out and margins were improving > went through their earnings calls and found the story of the product mix change > mapped out the value chain and tried to understand Sansera's moat in the new business they were focusing on > visited their facility to verify our thesis on the company.

Disclaimer: This is not a recommendation to buy or sell. We continue to hold it in our recommendation portfolio and may change our view at any point in time.

items.title: An elevator pitch on how the industrial gases industry works! You separate air into gases, or you buy rare gases and repackage them. You sell either f...
items.description_html:
An elevator pitch on how the industrial gases industry works!

You separate air into gases, or you buy rare gases and repackage them. You sell either from a plant you own (merchant) or from a plant you build inside a customer's factory (on-site).

On-site is a 15-20 year annuity at thin margins. A merchant is a spot market where the same molecule earns very different money depending on the gas, the distance, and who else is selling nearby.

The whole game is capital, location, and the ability to squeeze extra high-margin gas (argon, liquid) out of a plant you've already built.

But let’s get into interesting details about that -

What does the industry actually sell?

Strip away the chemistry and this is an air-separation business. A cryogenic plant is an Air Separation Unit, or ASU that chills atmospheric air until its components liquefy at their different boiling points, and pipes off oxygen, nitrogen and argon at high purity. Everyone in the industry runs broadly the same technology, so purity differences are marginal (roughly plus-or-minus 5%). The molecule is a commodity. Almost everything interesting happens around the molecule in how it's contracted, delivered, and priced.

The demand base has historically been the heavy stuff: steel and metals, autos, pharma, healthcare, and a thin slice of chemicals and F&B. What's changing the growth story is the sunrise demand from solar and semiconductors, which pull large volumes of nitrogen and, in semis, demand purity that cheaper suppliers struggle to hit. That single shift is why every player in the country is pouring capital into new capacity at the same time.

The top four global MNCs Linde, INOX Air Products, Air Water India and Air Liquide India control roughly 80% of the market.

Below them sit regional, owner-driven players (Ellenbarrie, Vayu, Shree Ram Oxygas and similar) who have been around 10–15 years and whose space widened after COVID, when oxygen subsidies pulled local capital in.

Now let’s understand the 2 engines in this industry separately > on-site vs merchant

Everything downstream flows from one fork in the road: do you build the plant inside the customer's factory, or near a cluster of customers and truck the gas out? These are two genuinely different businesses with different economics, different customers, and different personalities.

> On-site - An anchor customer, usually a large steel plant, issues an RFQ saying, in effect, we need ~1,100–1,800 tonnes of gas a day flowing into our furnace. A supplier builds and operates an ASU on their premises under a Build-Own-Operate (BOO) contract running 15–20 years. The revenue is fixed and stable, so it's underwritten on a modest return — players will accept an operating margin of roughly 10–12%, sometimes pricing the whole thing to a ~10–15% IRR. It is deliberately boring money.

Why fight so hard for boring money? Because it's stable, long-dated and defensive with a 15–20 year foothold that also keeps a rival out of that customer. Contracts signed before roughly 2016–18 carried fatter margins and some still run (a few end around 2035), but the new-build market is now openly competitive on price.

> Merchant business - Here you own the plant, liquefy the output, and sell it as liquid, bulk or cylinders to whoever's within reach. Margins are structurally better but volatile: liquid/bulk runs a ~20–25% bottom line, while cylinder and specialty can reach ~40%. The catch is geography. Oxygen and nitrogen are cheap and heavy, so you can't economically truck them much beyond ~200–300 km before distribution cost (typically 10–12% of revenue) eats you alive. You plant an ASU, draw a 200–300 km radius, and fight for that circle.

The reason branded MNCs earn ~40–45% at the top while a strong regional player earns ~35% isn't a secret formula rather it's scale and mix. A Linde or INOX moves 4,000–5,000 TPD daily; a regional player moves 250–300 TPD. At a small scale, tender-driven medical demand keeps margins decent. But to scale from 300 TPD to 3,000–4,000 TPD you must chase the lower-margin sectors that make up the bulk of the market and that's exactly where pricing and margin pressure begin.

The value chain, end to end

Follow a molecule of oxygen from the atmosphere to the customer and you can see where value is captured and where it leaks.

Stage 1 - Build the plant (the capital gate)
This is a capital-intensive, power-intensive industry, and the entry cost is the first moat. A modest 200–250 TPD on-site plant needs at least INR 300–400 crore of initial capex. Core components are compressors, cold boxes that have to be imported; India makes none of them. Only fabrication and storage tanks (INOX, Cryolor, VRV) are domestic. Build time runs 16–24 months per ASU

Stage 2 - Choose your engineering partner (the quiet moat)
Who actually builds the plant is becoming the real differentiator. The MNCs carry in-house EPC muscle - Linde has Linde Engineering, INOX leans on Air Products' US technology which lets them build large, reliable ASUs and win the technically demanding jobs.
Regional players without that engineering wing increasingly tie up with Chinese OEMs on a sale-of-equipment basis: the Chinese firm builds and exits, and the local player does the O&M. It's cheaper (a 200 TPD plant runs ~INR 100–120 crore via a Chinese vendor vs ~INR 150–200 crore via an MNC), but blue-chip steelmakers (Tata, JSW, SAIL, AM/NS) often won't allow a Chinese machine where they're underwriting 15–20 years of reliability, power efficiency and capital backup, and they pay up for it.

The cost-vs-capability gap
> MNC plant, 200 TPD: ~INR 150–200 crore — technology, reliability, blue-chip acceptance.
> Chinese plant, 200 TPD: ~INR 100–120 crore — cost-optimised, favoured by smaller / secondary steel and rolling mills.
> No Indian regulation restricts Chinese ASUs, so the split is driven purely by which customer is buying.

Stage 3 - Extract the by-products (where margin hides)
A basic ASU makes oxygen and nitrogen. To pull argon you must bolt on a separate argon-recovery column and here's the quirk: that column costs roughly the same whether the plant is small or large, but a small 200 TPD ASU yields only ~5–6 TPD of argon while a big ASU yields 50–60 TPD. The capital-to-recovery maths favours scale heavily, yet argon's economics are so attractive that even smaller players are now installing the column anyway.

Stage 4 - Distribute (the tyranny of distance)
Oxygen and nitrogen are regional products which are heavy, cheap, and uneconomic beyond ~300 km. Argon is a national product valuable enough to ship across the country, though distribution then runs ~17–18% of revenue rather than 10–12%. This distinction quietly shapes the entire competitive map: oxygen/nitrogen competition is local and radius-bound, while argon competition is national and cyclical.

How to judge any player in this industry?
Pulling the mechanics together, a handful of questions separate a structurally strong operator from a fragile one regardless of the name on the door.

> Capacity trajectory: Can they actually double liquid capacity? You can't sell a molecule if you can't make expansion of 200 TPD takes 1.5 - 2 years, not six months.

> Mix quality: How much on-site annuity vs volatile merchant? How much argon and by-product upside are they extracting per plant?

> Engineering independence: In-house EPC, or dependent on Chinese OEMs who build and exit? This gates which customers they can win.

> Geographic competition: Are their plants in pockets with few rivals inside the 300 km radius, or in contested western/central India?

> Blue-chip acceptance: Can they clear the reliability/purity bar for Tata, JSW, AM/NS, and semiconductors or are they confined to secondary, cost-driven demand?

> Cycle timing: Are they adding capacity into the current glut, and can their balance sheet and geography absorb 2–3 years of merchant price erosion before demand catches up?

Dislaimer - not a recommendation to buy/sell

Creative Newtech has done an interesting acquisition, transforming from a distributor to a manufacturer of an integrated surveillance technology platform.

Creative Newtech has approved the acquisition of 100% of Infinova (India) for up to US$4 million, marking a strategic shift beyond distribution into surveillance technology manufacturing.

The acquisition brings Infinova's India operations, brand rights, technical expertise, experienced workforce, and local assembly & manufacturing facility, providing Creative Newtech with immediate execution capabilities.

More importantly, the deal lays the foundation for a 'Make in India' surveillance platform, enabling the company to build proprietary products, strengthen after-sales support, and reduce dependence on third-party distribution.

The transaction also accelerates Creative's transition from a distribution-led business to an integrated, technology-led surveillance solutions provider, giving it greater control over manufacturing, product ownership, and margins.

The company holds all the relevant licenses from Gem, BIS, and STQC, enabling it to access the government portal. STQC shifts 22% market share from Chinese to Indian brands

This is more than an acquisition—it is a business model transformation, positioning Creative Newtech to move up the value chain from distributing surveillance products to designing, assembling, and manufacturing them under a 'Make in India' strategy.

Creative NewTech trades at 18 PE vs Prizor Vtech 42PE vs Aditya Infotech 110PE

items.description_html:
RT Sagar Awatade
I don't know who else to tell this to, so I am going to tell my story here.

Every day is a struggle for a young business, but the last few months have been harder than usual.

We are a small Indian company. For more than ten years we have been building a homegrown brand in a product category dominated by big foreign players.

There are almost no Indian names in this space. We set out to be one.

We started in 2014. Over the years we began making parts in India instead of just importing, and we started selling in the US, Dubai, Nepal, Malaysia and South Africa.

We showed up at global trade fairs to represent an Indian brand on the world stage.

In 2023 we changed the import code we use for our product. We did not do this quietly. Every shipment was declared. Nothing was hidden. We didn't invent our approach.

We followed written professional advice and the way this product is treated in markets around the world.

And now we are facing a government demand running into tens of crores in duty recovery and penalties, plus personal penalties on the founders and even on an employee.

For a company our size, this is not a fine we can pay and move on from. This ends us.

We have not run from any of this. I am not built like that. It is not how I was raised. We have written to the authorities, met officials in person, and we have now filed a writ in the High Court.

All we are asking for is a fair treatment.

I set out to build in India and sell to the world. I am asking only that the system back honest founders trying to compete globally, instead of breaking them.

The process is the process, and it exists for a reason. But process should not feel like punishment.

From where I am standing today, it does.
I am not giving up. I have worked too hard for this. If you have read this far, please share it. If you know someone who can help, point them my way. Help me get the word out.

items.title: Agentic routing is such an interesting study. Built a basic agent that does planning on Opus 4 but reasons on 4.6 through a tool call (skill call). Du...
items.description_html: Agentic routing is such an interesting study. Built a basic agent that does planning on Opus 4 but reasons on 4.6 through a tool call (skill call). Due to lack of document grounding, I embedded corpus into system prompt. Worked well. Second stage, enabled managed RAG for grounding & agent stated skipping tool call entirely, no skill calls. It treated grounded data as a higher evidence deterministic choice & skipped skill call. Tweaked tool description, still no skill call. Changed skill description matching to tool call & bingo!! Agent skipped grounding, entered planning mode & made a tool call. Evals for Agentic behavior is literally out paces everything in this field. What's your such key learning from a recent build?

items.title: A lot of defense to IT SIs right now is based on assumption that enterprise clients will not open their systems, data & processes to external AI solut...
items.description_html: A lot of defense to IT SIs right now is based on assumption that enterprise clients will not open their systems, data & processes to external AI solutions (Claude, OpenAi). However, this defense collapses the moment we have a precedence from a big enterprise opening up just the way enterprises opened up to cloud after a decade long friction. The moment this starts happening, the JVs OpenAi & Claude have formed will make a killing. And, what will take this wall down? For e.g., enterprises are currently very upset after SAP API policy that prohibited clients from using their own data & sending it to external tools via APIs to architect a solution outside of SAP. This can be the 1st hammer in the wall. One wrong step & clients will find ways to disconnect with enterprise OEMs & will be willing to trust(with an agreement perhaps) likes of Claude & OpenAi. The moment this happens, it is done!! This is the biggest risk I foresee.
